**Course:** Ascends 2.5 cm in front of the medial malleolus, along the medial aspect of the tibia with the saphenous nerve. Passes posterior to the medial condyles of the tibia and femur. Runs posterior to the patella and ascends along the medial side of the femur. Pierces the cribriform fascia and passes through the saphenous opening. Drains into the femoral vein after piercing the femoral sheath.

blocks.text: Clinical Aspects

items.text: **Venesection:** Performed at the ankle in emergencies. Care must be taken to avoid damaging the saphenous nerve (as it accompanies the vein).
**Coronary Bypass Surgery:** Commonly used as a graft for bypass surgery. The vein must be reversed to prevent its valves from obstructing blood flow in the graft.

blocks.text: The Gluteus medius and Gluteus minimus are responsible for the abduction and medial rotation of the thigh and are innervated by the superior gluteal nerve. A positive Trendelenburg test, which is indicated by a drop in the pelvic alignment when standing on one leg, is characteristic of a defect in these muscles. (as shown in the image) This condition suggests a superior gluteal nerve injury, which results in a lurching motion towards the side of the lesion.

**Posterior tibial artery:** The posterior tibial artery is located behind the medial malleolus and in front of the Achilles tendon. It runs posterior to the medial malleolus and can be palpated in this region.
Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Option B - Peroneal artery:** The peroneal artery (also known as the fibular artery) is located along the lateral side of the leg and is not found behind the medial malleolus. It supplies the lateral compartment of the leg.

**Option C - Anterior tibial artery:** The anterior tibial artery runs down the anterior part of the leg, in front of the interosseous membrane, and becomes the dorsalis pedis artery at the ankle. It is not located behind the medial malleolus.
**Option D - Dorsalis pedis artery:** The dorsalis pedis artery is located on the dorsum (top) of the foot, not behind the medial malleolus.

blocks.text: Pain in the back of the thigh and leg after lifting heavy weights is most commonly associated with the S2 nerve root. The S2 nerve root contributes to the sensation in the posterior aspect of the thigh and leg and can be affected by conditions such as sciatica or disc herniation.
Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Option A - L4:** The L4 nerve root typically affects the anterior and medial aspect of the thigh, as well as the medial side of the leg and foot. It is less likely to be associated with pain specifically in the back of the thigh and leg.

**Option B - L5:** The L5 nerve root affects the lateral aspect of the leg and the dorsum of the foot. While it can cause pain radiating down the leg, it is not typically associated with pain specifically in the back of the thigh.

**Option C - S1:** The S1 nerve root affects the posterior and lateral aspects of the leg and the heel. Pain in the back of the thigh and leg can be related to S1, but S2 is more directly associated with the described pain after heavy lifting.

blocks.text: This nerve supplies the adductor muscles of the thigh, which are part of the hybrid muscle group that is spared in sciatica. The obturator nerve is primarily responsible for innervating the adductor muscles (adductor longus, adductor brevis, adductor magnus, and gracilis) which are not affected in sciatica, as sciatica mainly involves the sciatic nerve and its branches.
Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Option A - Femoral Nerve:** This nerve innervates the quadriceps and other muscles of the anterior thigh. In sciatica, the femoral nerve is generally not directly involved, but the tender hamstrings are more related to the sciatic nerve and its branches.

**Option B - Common Peroneal Nerve:** This is a branch of the sciatic nerve, and sciatica can affect it, leading to symptoms like foot drop. It does not provide significant innervation to the hybrid muscle group that is mentioned in this context.

**Option D - Tibial Nerve:** This is another branch of the sciatic nerve, and it innervates the posterior compartment of the leg and the plantar aspect of the foot. It is involved in sciatica and is not spared in this condition.

**Option D - Popliteal artery:** To palpate the popliteal artery, ask the patient to lie down on their stomach or to sit with their legs hanging off the edge of the exam table. Flex the knee to about 90 degrees. Use your fingers to locate the popliteal fossa, which is the small depression behind the knee joint. Feel for the pulsation of the artery in the middle of the fossa. Press your fingers gently into the popliteal fossa and feel for the pulsation of the artery.

Sciatic Nerve Origin and Course

The thickest nerve in the body. Arises from the ventral rami of L4–S3 spinal nerves. Exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis and descends between the greater trochanter and ischial tuberosity along the back of the thigh.
Divides into the tibial and common peroneal nerves above the popliteal fossa.
Distribution

items.text: **Motor:**
**Undivided Trunk:** Supplies all muscles of the back of the thigh (hip extension, knee flexion).
**Tibial Nerve:** Innervates leg muscles (flexion) and foot muscles (plantar flexion).
**Common Peroneal Nerve:** Supplies leg muscles (dorsiflexion).
**Sensory:**
**Tibial Nerve:** Supplies skin on the back of the calf, heel, lateral border of the foot, and sole.
**Common Peroneal Nerve:** Supplies skin on the anterolateral and lateral surfaces of the leg and dorsum of the foot (except for the deep peroneal nerve area).

blocks.text: Clinical correlation
**Injury of the sciatic nerve:** Causes: Penetrating wounds, posterior hip dislocation, pelvic fractures, total hip replacement, misplaced injections in the gluteal region.
**Clinical Features:** Inability to extend the thigh and flex the knee (hamstring paralysis).
Loss of all movements below the knee (foot drop) leading to flail foot and high-stepping gait. Loss of sensation on the back of the thigh, entire leg, and foot (except for the saphenous nerve area).

**Sciatica:** Shooting pain along the sciatic nerve distribution (buttock, posterior thigh, lateral leg, dorsum of the foot). Compression/irritation of L4–S3 spinal nerve roots due to herniated lumbar discs.
**Neuropathy:** Entrapment in the piriformis muscle can lead to piriformis syndrome.

The Lisfranc ligament connects the medial cuneiform to the base of the second metatarsal. It is a strong oblique ligament that stabilises the tarsometatarsal (TMT) joint and prevents excessive movement between the midfoot and forefoot. Injury to this ligament leads to a Lisfranc injury, which involves displacement of the second metatarsal and can result in significant midfoot instability.

**Anatomy:** The Lisfranc joint is formed by the metatarsal bones (M1 to M5) and the tarsal bones (cuneiform C1 to C3 and cuboid). The Lisfranc ligament is a 3 part structure that joins the medial cuneiform to the 2nd metatarsal. Interdigitating joints and strong ligaments support the five tarsometatarsal (TMT) joints. The second metatarsal base fits into a recess formed by the medial, intermediate, and lateral cuneiforms.

**Injury Mechanism:** Dislocations are rare and typically arise from twisting or crushing injuries, with the foot buckling at the midfoot–forefoot junction. Often considered high-energy injuries, leading to extensive damage to the foot. The direction of forefoot dislocation is not useful for treatment guidance or outcome prediction.

**Clinical Features:** Suspect TMT dislocation or fracture-dislocation in patients with foot pain and swelling after high-velocity impacts (e.g., car accidents, falls). About 20–30% of these injuries are initially missed. Obvious deformity usually only occurs with severe injuries.

**Imaging:** X-rays: Interpretation can be challenging; systematic examination is crucial. Focus on the alignment of the second and fourth metatarsals (oblique view): The medial edge of the second metatarsal should align with the medial edge of the second cuneiform. The medial edge of the fourth metatarsal should align with the medial side of the cuboid. A true lateral view may show dorsal displacement of the second metatarsal base.
**Advanced Imaging:** If fracture-dislocation is suspected, stress views may help, but a CT scan is more effective for assessing the extent of injury.
**Treatment:**

items.text: **Undisplaced Sprains:** Require 4–6 weeks of cast or boot immobilization.

**Subluxation or Dislocation:** Accurate reduction is necessary, often achieved through traction and manipulation under anesthesia. The position is stabilized with percutaneous K-wires or screws, followed by cast immobilization (non-weight-bearing for 6–8 weeks).

**Open Reduction:** If closed reduction fails, open reduction is essential. Exposure of the second metatarsal base via a longitudinal incision for joint manipulation. Fixation with K-wires or screws, followed by immobilization.

blocks.text: **Complications:** Compartment Syndrome: A tense, swollen foot may indicate serious compartment syndrome. Measure intracompartmental pressures if suspected. Prompt decompression through surgical incisions is critical; the wound is left open until swelling subsides.

items.text: **Chopart ligament (option A):** Related to the Chopart joint, which is the midtarsal (transverse tarsal) joint, connecting the hindfoot (talus and calcaneus) to the midfoot (navicular and cuboid). Not involved in the medial cuneiform–second metatarsal connection.

**Spring ligament (option B):** Also called the plantar calcaneonavicular ligament, it connects the calcaneus to the navicular and supports the medial longitudinal arch of the foot. Does not link the medial cuneiform to the second metatarsal.
**Deltoid ligament (option D):** A strong medial ankle ligament, stabilising the talus within the ankle mortise. It is unrelated to the tarsometatarsal joints.

blocks.text: A positive Trendelenburg test indicates weakness of the hip abductors, specifically the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus. These muscles are innervated by the superior gluteal nerve. In this case, the right-sided Trendelenburg sign means the right gluteus medius and minimus are weak, which occurs due to damage to the right superior gluteal nerve.

Trendelenberg sign: When the body's weight is balanced on one leg, the gluteal muscles on the supported side help elevate the opposite, unsupported side of the pelvis. However, if there is a malfunction in the abductor mechanism, the Sound side sinks, which is referred to as a positive Trendelenburg sign (uncompensated).

This sign indicates issues with hip abductors, such as paralysis of the gluteus medius and minimus; problems with the fulcrum, including congenital or pathological hip dislocations; and concerns related to body weight, such as an unhealed fracture of the femoral neck.

When patients with the gluteus medius and minimus paralysis walk, they have a characteristic lurching gait ie, during the single leg supporting phase of walking, there is leaning of the trunk to the affected side known as the compensated Trendelenburg sign. Duck waddling gait is seen when both the sides are affected.

items.text: **Right inferior gluteal nerve (option A):** The inferior gluteal nerve innervates the gluteus maximus, which is responsible for hip extension, not abduction. Damage here would cause difficulty rising from a seated position or climbing stairs, not a Trendelenburg sign.
**Left superior gluteal nerve (option C):** If the left superior gluteal nerve were affected, the right hip would drop when standing on the left leg, not the right leg.
**Left inferior gluteal nerve (option D):** The inferior gluteal nerve does not control hip abduction, and the left-sided nerve would not cause a right-sided Trendelenburg sign.

This nerve provides motor innervation to the gluteus maximus, which is the largest muscle in the buttocks and plays a significant role in movements such as hip extension and external rotation.

blocks.text: Answer B - Saphenous nerve

The saphenous nerve is a purely sensory branch of the femoral nerve (L3-L4) that supplies sensation to the medial leg and foot. During coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), the great saphenous vein (GSV) is commonly harvested for the bypass procedure.

Since the saphenous nerve runs alongside the GSV in the leg, it is highly susceptible to injury during vein harvesting, leading to paresthesia and sensory loss over the medial aspect of the leg and foot.

items.text: **Superficial peroneal nerve (option A):** Provides sensory innervation to the anterolateral lower leg and dorsum of the foot. Unlikely to be affected in CABG as it is located in the lateral compartment of the leg.

**Femoral nerve (option C):** Provides motor innervation to the anterior thigh muscles and sensory innervation to the anterior and medial thigh. Injury would cause weakness of quadriceps and loss of knee jerk reflex, which is not described in the question.
**Sural nerve (option D):** Provides sensory innervation to the lateral foot and posterolateral calf. Not involved in medial leg and foot sensation, making it an unlikely option.

The peroneus longus muscle, also known as fibularis longus, is located on the lateral side of the leg. It is primarily responsible for eversion (turning outward) of the foot, not inversion. Eversion is the opposite movement of inversion and involves turning the sole of the foot outward.

**Option B. Tibialis posterior:** The tibialis posterior muscle is located on the back (posterior) side of the leg. It is a powerful muscle that contributes to both inversion and plantar flexion (pointing) of the foot. It helps to maintain the arch of the foot and provides stability during walking and running.

**Option D. Extensor hallucis longus:** The extensor hallucis longus muscle is located on the front (anterior) side of the leg. It is responsible for dorsiflexion of the foot and extension of the big toe. While it does not directly contribute to inversion of the foot, it plays a role in maintaining the foot's position during various movements.

items.text: **1 (Gluteus maximus) (Option A):** Incorrect – Gluteus maximus is responsible for hip extension. Injury causes difficulty in rising from a seated position but does not cause a lurching gait.

**3 (Piriformis) (Option C):** Incorrect – Piriformis primarily functions in hip external rotation. Injury leads to piriformis syndrome, which causes sciatica-like pain but does not cause a lurching gait.

blocks.text: Foot drop is commonly caused by damage to the common peroneal nerve, also known as the common fibular nerve. The common peroneal nerve innervates the muscles responsible for ankle dorsiflexion and foot eversion. Damage to this nerve can occur due to various factors such as trauma, compression, nerve entrapment, or underlying medical conditions.
Incorrect Option:

items.text: **Option B: Femoral nerve:** The femoral nerve primarily innervates the muscles of the anterior thigh, including the quadriceps femoris muscle group. It is not directly responsible for ankle dorsiflexion or foot drop.

**Option C: Tibial nerve:** The tibial nerve innervates the muscles of the posterior compartment of the leg, including the calf muscles that are involved in ankle plantar flexion. Damage to the tibial nerve may result in difficulty with plantar flexion but is not a common cause of foot drop.

**Option D: Sciatic nerve:** The sciatic nerve is the largest nerve in the body and consists of two components: the tibial nerve and the common peroneal nerve. While damage to the sciatic nerve can potentially cause foot drop, it is more specifically attributed to damage to the common peroneal nerve, which is a branch of the sciatic nerve.

**Dorsalis pedis artery (Option C):** The dorsalis pedis artery is located on the dorsal (top) aspect of the foot, specifically between the first and second metatarsal bones. It is not palpated between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal tendon.
**Popliteal artery (Option D):** The popliteal artery is located behind the knee joint in the popliteal fossa. It is not palpated between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal tendon.

blocks.text: The neurovascular bundle refers to a grouping of blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatic vessels that travel together in a common sheath. In the leg, the neurovascular bundle is absent in the posterior superficial compartment.
Incorrect options:

items.text: **Option A Lateral compartment:** The lateral compartment of the leg contains the fibularis (peroneal) muscles and their associated blood vessels and nerves. While the specific arrangement of the neurovascular bundle may vary, it is generally present in the lateral compartment.

**Option C: Posterior deep compartment:** The posterior deep compartment of the leg contains the deep muscles, such as the tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, and flexor hallucis longus, along with their associated blood vessels and nerves. The neurovascular bundle is typically present in this compartment.

**Option D: Anterior compartment:** The anterior compartment of the leg contains the muscles responsible for dorsiflexion of the foot and toe extension, such as the tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus. It also houses the anterior tibial artery and its branches, as well as the deep peroneal nerve. The neurovascular bundle is present in this compartment.

blocks.text: Abduction at the hip joint, which refers to moving the leg away from the midline of the body, is primarily performed by the gluteus medius muscle. The gluteus medius is a broad, thick muscle located on the lateral aspect of the hip. It acts as a powerful abductor of the hip joint and plays a crucial role in maintaining stability during activities such as walking and running.
Incorrect options:

items.text: **Option A. Gluteus maximus:** The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle of the buttocks and primarily functions in extending and externally rotating the hip joint. While it can assist in abduction, it is not the primary muscle responsible for this movement.
**Option C. Obturator internus:** The obturator internus is a deep muscle of the hip that acts as an external rotator of the hip joint. It does not contribute significantly to hip abduction.

**Option D. Quadratus femoris:** The quadratus femoris is a deep muscle of the hip that assists in hip joint stabilization and contributes to hip rotation. It is not a primary muscle involved in hip abduction.

blocks.text: **Radial head:** The radial head is a rounded bony structure located at the proximal end of the radius bone. It articulates with the capitulum of the humerus to form the radiocapitular joint, allowing rotational movements of the forearm.
Incorrect options:

items.text: **Option A - Capitulum:** The capitulum is a bony prominence located on the distal end of the humerus. It articulates with the head of the radius to form the radio capitular joint.

**Option B - Olecranon:** The olecranon is a bony process located at the proximal end of the ulna, forming the prominent bony tip of the elbow. It serves as the insertion point for the triceps brachii muscle.

**Option C - Trochlea:** The trochlea is a structure located on the distal end of the humerus and plays a crucial role in the formation of the elbow joint. It articulates with the trochlear notch of the ulna, allowing flexion and extension movements of the forearm.

blocks.text: The peroneus longus muscle, also known as the fibularis longus muscle, is located on the lateral side of the leg. It plays a significant role in foot eversion. When the peroneus longus contracts, it pulls the foot outward, causing eversion.
Incorrect options:

items.text: **Option A: Extensor digitorum:** The extensor digitorum muscle is located on the anterior aspect of the leg and primarily functions to extend the digits (toes) and dorsiflex the foot. It is not directly involved in foot eversion.

**Option C: Tibialis anterior:** The tibialis anterior muscle is located on the anterior aspect of the leg. Its primary action is dorsiflexion and inversion of the foot. It is not directly involved in foot eversion.

**Option D: Tibialis posterior:** The tibialis posterior muscle is located on the posterior aspect of the leg. Its primary action is plantarflexion and inversion of the foot. It works in the opposite direction of foot eversion.

blocks.text: The biceps femoris muscle is innervated by the tibial and common peroneal nerves. The tibial nerve supplies the long head of the biceps femoris, while the common peroneal nerve supplies the short head. Therefore, the tibial and common peroneal nerves do supply the biceps femoris muscle
Incorrect options:

items.text: **Option A: Gracilis:** The gracilis muscle is primarily innervated by the obturator nerve, not the tibial or common peroneal nerve. Therefore, the tibial and common peroneal nerves do not supply the gracilis muscle

**Option C: Adductor longus:** The adductor longus muscle is primarily innervated by the obturator nerve, not the tibial or common peroneal nerve. Thus, the tibial and common peroneal nerves do not supply the adductor longus muscle.

**Option D: Adductor magnus:** The adductor magnus muscle is primarily innervated by the obturator and sciatic nerves. The sciatic nerve, which is composed of the tibial and common peroneal nerves, supplies the posterior part of the adductor magnus. However, the tibial and common peroneal nerves alone do not supply the adductor magnus muscle.

blocks.text: The action of the muscle attached to the marked area is abduction. The muscle attached to the lateral surface of the greater trochanter is the gluteus Medius muscle. It plays a crucial role in the abduction of the hip joint. Abduction refers to the movement of a body part away from the midline of the body. In the case of the hip joint, abduction involves moving the leg away from the body's midline, out to the side.
Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Option A:** Flexion refers to bending or decreasing the angle between two body parts. The action of the gluteus Medius muscle is not primarily related to flexion.

**Option B:** Adduction refers to the movement of a body part towards the midline of the body. The gluteus Medius muscle is not directly involved in adduction but rather acts as an antagonist to the adductor muscles.
**Option D:** Extension refers to straightening or increasing the angle between two body parts. The gluteus Medius muscle does not primarily contribute to extension but rather to abduction.

blocks.text: In the provided diagram, the marked tendon corresponds to the Extensor hallucis longus. The Extensor hallucis longus is a muscle located in the anterior compartment of the leg. It originates from the middle third of the fibula and inserts onto the base of the distal phalanx of the great toe. Its main action is to extend (dorsiflex) the great toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint and assist in dorsiflexion of the ankle joint.
Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Option B. Flexor hallucis longus:** This muscle is located in the posterior compartment of the leg and is responsible for flexing the great toe.
**Option C. Extensor digitorum longus:** This muscle is also located in the anterior compartment of the leg and is responsible for extending (dorsiflexing) the lateral four toes.
**Option D. Tibialis anterior:** This muscle is located in the anterior compartment of the leg and is responsible for dorsiflexion and inversion of the foot

blocks.text: Bulbus cordis is located at the cranial end of the developing heart tube, not the caudal end.

**Formation of Heart Tubes:** The endothelial heart tube is derived from the splanchnopleuric mesoderm, located near the pericardial cavity. (Option A) Initially, the heart appears as right and left endothelial heart tubes. These tubes fuse to form a single heart tube.
The heart tube has 5 dilatations, which are:

items.text: Truncus arteriosus
Bulbus cordis
Primitive ventricle
Primitive atrium
Sinus venosus

blocks.text: Sinus venosus is located at the caudal (venous) end of the primitive heart tube. It consists of a body with two prolongations known as the right and left horns. Right horn: Forms smooth part of the right atrium (sinus venarum). Left horn: Forms coronary sinus.
Each horn receives blood from three veins:

items.text: Vitelline vein
Umbilical vein
Common cardinal vein

blocks.text: Bulbus cordis is the cranial most part of the developing heart tube. (Option C) Forms outflow (smooth) parts of the right ventricle (conus arteriosus) and left ventricle (aortic vestibule).
**Primitive ventricle:** Forms inflow (rough) parts of both ventricles.
**Primitive atrium:** Forms trabeculated part of the right and left atrium.
**Truncus arteriosus:** Forms ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk. (Option B)

**Formation of Transverse Pericardial Sinus:** Heart Tube Folding: Brings the arterial and venous ends closer together. Disappearance of the dorsal mesocardium creates the transverse sinus of the pericardium. (Option D) Parietal and visceral layers of the serous pericardium become continuous at the arterial and venous ends of the heart.
Pericardium forms two tubes: One enclosing the aorta and pulmonary trunk. Other enclosing the SVC, IVC, and four pulmonary veins. Two tubes are separated by the transverse sinus of the pericardium.
The posterior part of the membranous septum separates the left ventricle from the right atrium, not the right ventricle from the left atrium.
Formation of Interventricular Septum
The interventricular septum consists of three parts:

items.text: Muscular part
Bulbar part
Membranous part

blocks.text: 1. Muscular Part

Septum grows upward from the floor of the bulboventricular cavity, dividing it into right and left halves. (Option A) This growth is driven by passive dilation and hemodynamic forces. Septum fuses with the atrioventricular (AV) cushions (septum intermedium).
Interventricular foramen forms between the two ventricles at the upper margin of the septum and is eventually closed by the septum intermedium and proximal bulbar septum. (Option D)
2. Bulbar Part

Two bulbar ridges (right and left) arise from the wall of the bulboventricular cavity. These ridges fuse to form the proximal bulbar septum, which grows downward toward the muscular septum but leaves a gap. (Option B)
3. Membranous Part
The gap between the muscular septum and the bulbar septum is filled by tissue from the AV cushions and bulbar ridges. Membranous septum consists of:

items.text: Anterior part: Separates the right and left ventricles.
Posterior part: Separates the left ventricle from the right atrium. (Option C)

blocks.text: Mechanism of Septal Formation
Interventricular septum is likely formed by the downward enlargement of the right and left ventricular cavities on either side of the septum, rather than by active septal growth itself.

Ductus arteriosus allows most blood from the right ventricle to bypass the lungs by shunting it directly into the aorta, ensuring efficient delivery of oxygenated blood to the fetal brain and upper body.
Fetal Circulation:

items.text: **Oxygenated Blood Flow:** Placenta → Umbilical Vein → Ductus Venosus (bypasses liver) → Inferior Vena Cava → Right Atrium → Foramen Ovale → Left Atrium → Left Ventricle → Ascending Aorta → Oxygen to head, neck, and upper limbs

**Deoxygenated Blood Flow:** Superior Vena Cava (SVC) → Right Atrium → Right Ventricle → Pulmonary Trunk → Ductus Arteriosus (bypass pulmonary circulation) → Descending Aorta → Lower body → Umbilical Arteries → Placenta (for oxygenation)

blocks.text: Peculiarities of Fetal Circulation

items.text: **Ductus Venosus:** Directs blood to the inferior vena cava, bypassing the liver and preserving oxygen content. (Option A)
**Foramen Ovale:** Allows equal distribution of blood to both sides of the heart, ensuring more oxygenated blood reaches vital organs in the upper body. (Option C)
**Ductus Arteriosus:** Directs blood from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, bypassing the lungs and allowing blood to flow to the placenta for oxygenation. (Option B)

blocks.text: More oxygenated blood flows to the upper limbs, resulting in longer upper limbs compared to lower limbs in the fetus.

**Umbilical vein (Option D):** carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus, but it doesn’t play a role in shunting blood past the lungs. Its function is to deliver oxygenated blood to the fetal circulation through the ductus venosus.

A machinery-like murmur in a neonate along with cyanosis and rapid breathing suggests patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). PDA is a fetal vessel connecting the pulmonary artery to the aorta that normally closes soon after birth. If it remains open (patent), it causes a left-to-right shunt (oxygenated blood from the aorta flows back into the pulmonary artery), leading to volume overload in the lungs, causing cyanosis and respiratory distress.

Persistent foramen ovale typically causes a different murmur and shunting pattern; closure of ductus venosus affects liver blood flow; malrotation of great arteries affects vessel positioning, not shunting or murmur.
Changes in the Circulation at Birth
Umbilical Arteries
Thick muscle walls of the umbilical arteries contract immediately after birth, occluding their lumen. This prevents the loss of fetal blood into the placenta.
Umbilical Vein and Ductus Venosus
Lumen of the umbilical vein and ductus venosus occludes a few minutes after birth, allowing time for fetal blood from the placenta to return to the fetus.
Ductus Arteriosus

Closes initially due to muscle contraction in the vessel wall, and later, intimal proliferation permanently obliterates the lumen, redirecting blood from the right ventricle to the lungs for oxygenation.
Pulmonary Vessels
Increase in size, allowing more blood to reach the left atrium from the lungs, increasing left atrial pressure.
Foramen Ovale

Increased pressure in the left atrium (due to lung circulation) and reduced pressure in the right atrium (due to cessation of placental blood flow) lead to the closure of the valve of the foramen ovale.
Fetal Circulatory Shunts and Their Changes After Birth

rows: Shunts blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta, bypassing pulmonary circulation.
Shunts blood from the right atrium to the left atrium
Shunts blood from the umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava, bypassing the liver
Carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus
Carries deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta

Proximal part: Superior vesical artery
Distal part: Medial umbilical ligaments

blocks.text: Persistent foramen ovale (Option A) allows the shunting of blood from the right atrium to the left atrium, bypassing the lungs. While it can cause cyanosis, the clinical presentation usually doesn't include a machinery murmur, and it is typically asymptomatic or mild compared to PDA.
Closure of ductus venosus (Option C) occurs normally after birth and redirects blood flow, but it does not cause shunting or significant symptoms like cyanosis or a murmur.

**Malrotation of the great arteries (Option D):** is a form of congenital heart defect that can cause cyanosis, but it would typically be detected earlier, often with profound cyanosis from birth. Unlike PDA, it does not present with a machinery-like murmur and does not involve a left-to-right shunt.
The absence of spiral aorticopulmonary septum (AP septum) is a pathologic finding in truncus arteriosus (TA).

**Formation of the Bulbus Cordis:** The bulbus cordis is the cranial-most region of the primitive heart tube, Originates from the cardiogenic area, a specialized mesoderm region cranial to the prochordal plate. Divides into 3 parts:

items.text: **Proximal one-third:** Merges with the primitive ventricle to form the bulboventricular chamber. Contributes to the trabeculated part of the right ventricle.

**Middle part (Conus Cordis):** Forms outflow tracts of both ventricles. Two septae are formed in this: proximal and distal bulbar septa. The proximal septum contributes to the interventricular septum. The distal septum divides the conus into the aortic vestibule and conus arteriosus.

**Distal part (Truncus Arteriosus):** Divides into ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk via the spiral aortopulmonary septum Spiral septum is formed by the fusion of the right superior and left inferior truncus swellings or cushions. Responsible for distributing blood to the body and lungs.

blocks.text: **Clinical Significance:** Persistent truncus arteriosus: Complete absence of spiral septum. (Option D)

**Ventricular Septal Defects (VSDs):** Result from incomplete closure of the interventricular septum, leading to holes in the ventricular wall. (Option C) Symptoms may include shortness of breath and an increased risk of infections.
**Tetralogy of Fallot:** Comprises four defects linked to abnormalities in the conus and truncus arteriosus:

items.text: VSD
Overriding aorta
Pulmonary stenosis (Option A)
Right ventricular hypertrophy

blocks.text: Can cause cyanosis and impede blood flow to the lungs.

**Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA):** Occurs when the aorta and pulmonary artery are switched due to errors in truncus arteriosus division. (Option B) Requires surgical intervention to correct blood flow issues.
Left horn of the sinus venosus regresses during development to form the coronary sinus, so a defect in this structure can result in an abnormal coronary sinus.
**Sinus Venosus:** Structure of Sinus Venosus Sinus venosus is the caudal (venous) end of the primitive heart tube, consisting of a body with right and left horns.
Each horn is connected to three major veins:

items.text: Vitelline vein (from the yolk sac)
Umbilical vein (from the placenta)
Common cardinal vein (from the body wall)

blocks.text: **Communication with Atrial Chamber:** Sinus venosus initially communicates with the primitive atrium through a wide sinoatrial orifice. Grooves appear on the lateral walls of the heart, partially separating the sinus venosus from the atrium.
**Regression of the Left Horn:** Left horn and its tributaries become reduced in size and become part of the coronary sinus.
**Fate of Right Horn (Option A):** Incorporated into the right atrium, forming the smooth-walled part of the right atrium (sinus venarum).
Fate of Sinus Venosus Tributaries

items.text: Right common cardinal vein becomes part of the superior vena cava. (Option C)
Right vitelline vein forms the terminal part of the inferior vena cava. (Option D)
Left horn regresses and becomes part of the coronary sinus. (Option B)
Left common cardinal vein forms the oblique vein of the left atrium.

blocks.text: The cardiac jelly is an acellular matrix that is secreted by the myocardium in the developing heart.
**Cardiac Jelly (CJ):** A gelatinous, cell-free extracellular matrix filling the myoendocardial space of the embryonic heart tube.
**Function:**

items.text: Acts as a hydraulic skeleton, providing structural support during early heart development. (Option A)
Facilitates end-systolic occlusion of the embryonic heart lumen, improving pumping efficiency. (Option B)
Stores elastic energy during systole, aiding the refilling phase of the heart. (Option C)

blocks.text: Septum primum (Label A) grows first and contributes to the division of the atria. The septum secundum (Label B) grows later and overlaps the septum primum, forming the foramen ovale, which allows right-to-left blood flow in fetal life.
Septum Primum

Formed as a sickle-shaped fold from the roof and dorsal wall of the primitive atrium due to pressure from the bulbus cordis. Grows downward toward the atrioventricular (AV) canal and septum intermedium, fusing with the latter.
Ostium Primum
Before the septum primum reaches and fuses with the septum intermedium, a gap (foramen primum) allows blood flow between the right and left atria.
Ostium Secundum
Upper part of the septum primum breaks down, creating a new gap (foramen secundum) before the foramen primum closes. The septum primum now has a free upper edge.
Septum Secundum
Grows down from the roof of the atrial chamber, to the right of the septum primum, overlapping the free upper edge of the septum primum as it grows.
Foramen Ovale Formation
Overlapping septa create the foramen ovale, allowing blood to flow from right to left atrium during fetal life, preventing left-to-right flow. Patent throughout fetal life.
Obliteration of Foramen Ovale

Post-birth, the left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs, increasing pressure in this chamber greater than the right atrium, causing fusion of the septum primum and septum secundum, closing the foramen ovale. Annulus ovalis (adults) corresponds to the lower free edge of the septum secundum, while the fossa ovalis represents the septum primum.
Ostium secundum defect is the most common significant ASD characterized by a large atrial opening.
Defects in Interatrial Septal Development

Atrial Septal Defect (ASD): Varies from total absence of the atrial septum to small openings, such as probe patency of the oval foramen. Most significant defect: Ostium secundum defect, characterized by a large opening between the left and right atria.
Causes:

items.text: Excessive cell death and resorption of the septum primum.
Inadequate development of the septum secundum.

blocks.text: Complete Absence of Atrial Septum
Known as common atrium or cor triloculare biventriculare. Result from complete failure of the septum primum and septum secundum to form.
Premature Closure of Foramen Ovale
It can occur during prenatal life. Results in:

items.text: Massive hypertrophy of the right atrium and ventricle.
Underdevelopment of the left side of the heart.
Often leads to death shortly after birth.

blocks.text: **Ostium primum defect (Option A):** Accounts for about 10% of septal defects and develops due to a deficiency in tissue near the atrioventricular valves, making it less common than ostium secundum.

**Sinus venosus defect (Option B):** is located outside the fossa ovalis on the right septal surface. It is associated with anomalous right upper pulmonary venous return rather than a large atrial opening between the atria.

**Coronary Sinus Defect (Option C):** is located in the wall separating the coronary sinus from the left atrium; it may be fenestrated or absent and does not create a significant opening between the left and right atria.
Limbus fossa ovalis is the raised ridge surrounding the fossa ovalis.

**Fossa Ovalis:** (Option C) Depressed area located in the lower portion of the right atrial side of the interatrial septum. Remnant of the foramen ovale. Septum primum which is on the left atrial side, forms the floor of the fossa ovalis.
**Limbus Fossa Ovalis:** (Option D) A raised ridge (annulus) that surrounds the perimeter of the fossa ovalis. It is formed from the septum secundum, an infolding of the atrial roof.
**Septum primum (Option A):** forms the floor of the fossa ovalis, not the raised ridge surrounding it.
**Septum secundum (Option B):** contributes to the formation of the limbus fossa ovalis but does not directly appear as a raised ridge itself.

The spiraling of the aorticopulmonary septum positions the pulmonary trunk anteriorly and to the left of the aorta. This arrangement is crucial for separating the pulmonary and systemic circulations. The bulbus cordis elongates into three segments:

items.text: Proximal part forms bulboventricular chamber
Middle part: Conus cordis (outflow tract)
Distal part (Truncus arteriosus) develops into the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk

blocks.text: Truncus arteriosus undergoes septation and spiraling. There are two swellings along the truncus arteriosus- truncal swellings distally and conal swellings proximally.

The truncal swellings, resembling endocardial cushions, divide the lumen into the proximal ascending aorta and the pulmonary trunk. The fusion of truncal and conal swellings establishes the pulmonary trunk’s origin from the right ventricle and the aorta’s origin from the left ventricle, with aortopulmonary valves forming at these fusion lines.
Spiraling of the septum allows the pulmonary trunk to cross anterior and to the left of the aorta. (Option C)
Failure of neural crest cells to migrate or disruptions to the aorticopulmonary septum leads to congenital heart disease
Septation defects:

items.text: **Persistent truncus arteriosus:** Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to form
**Tetralogy of Fallot:** Anterior and cephalad deviation of the aorticopulmonary septum. Comprises four defects linked to abnormalities:
VSD
Overriding aorta
Pulmonary stenosis
Right ventricular hypertrophy
**Double outlet right ventricle**

blocks.text: Spiraling defects:
**Transposition of the great vessels:** Positions of the aorta and pulmonary artery are switched due to errors in truncus arteriosus division.
**The pulmonary trunk moves posteriorly (Option A):** The pulmonary trunk moves anteriorly.

**The aorta moves to the right side of the body (Option B):** The aorta does end up in a more rightward position relative to the pulmonary trunk, but it does not specifically move to the right side of the body.
**There is no change in the position of either vessel (Option D):** The spiraling process specifically reorganizes the positions of the pulmonary trunk and aorta.

In this scenario, the newborn exhibits significant cyanosis and a single large vessel which is suggestive of persistent truncus arteriosus. It resulted from the failure of the conotruncal ridges to develop, which prevents the proper division of the outflow tracts into the aorta and pulmonary artery, leading to the mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.
Aorticopulmonary septum anomalies
1) Tetralogy of Fallot
Most common conotruncal heart defect. Cause: Due to unequal division of the conus and anterior displacement of the septum. (Option D) Features four cardiovascular issues:

items.text: Pulmonary infundibular stenosis
Overriding aorta
Ventricular septal defect (VSD)
Right ventricular hypertrophy

blocks.text: Tetralogy along with ASD is known as pentalogy of fallot. Common in individuals with Alagille syndrome (also features liver abnormalities and distinctive facial traits). Often associated with a JAG1 gene mutation affecting neural crest cells.
2) Persistent Truncus Arteriosus

Cause: Failure of conotruncal ridges to form. (Option B) Features: Leads to a single outflow tract and a defective interventricular septum. The truncus overrides both ventricles. Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood combine, with lung-bound blood entering systemic circulation. Results in congenital cyanotic heart disease.
3) Transposition of the Great Vessels

Cause: Occurs when the conotruncal septum fails to spiral correctly. (Option C) Features:s Aorta connects to the right ventricle, pulmonary artery connects to the left ventricle. Patients cannot survive because deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium through the superior and inferior vena cavae, then flows to the right ventricle and into the ascending aorta, bypassing the lungs completely. PDA is essential for survival, allowing blood flow to the lungs for oxygenation.
**Failure of the atrioventricular septum to form (Option A):** refers to atrioventricular septal defects, which involve issues in the separation of the atria and ventricles, not the outflow tracts.
The superior hemiazygos vein drains into the azygos vein at the level of the seventh thoracic vertebra.
Azygos Vein

The origin of the azygos vein can vary, often starting from the union of the right ascending lumbar vein and the right subcostal vein in the abdomen. It ascends through the aortic opening in the diaphragm, on the right side of the aorta. The vein continues to rise until it reaches the level of the fifth thoracic vertebra. At this level, the azygos vein arches forward above the root of the right lung. It drains into the posterior surface of the superior vena cava. (Option A ruled out)
**Tributaries:**

items.text: The eight lower right intercostal veins
The right superior intercostal vein
The superior and inferior hemiazygos veins
Mediastinal veins.
Pericardial veins
Right subcostal vein.
Right bronchial vein.
Right ascending lumbar vein.

blocks.text: If there is an obstruction of the SVC, the azygos vein acts as the primary collateral pathway to redirect blood from the upper half of the body to the IVC. (Option D ruled out)
Inferior Hemiazygos Vein

The inferior hemiazygos vein is formed by the union of the left ascending lumbar vein and the left subcostal vein in the abdomen. It ascends through the left crus of the diaphragm and, around the level of the eighth thoracic vertebra, it turns to the right to join the azygos vein, receiving tributaries from the lower left intercostal and mediastinal veins. (Option B ruled out)
Superior Hemiazygos Vein

The superior hemiazygos vein is created by the union of the left superior intercostal vein and the fourth to eighth intercostal veins. It drains into the azygos vein at the level of the seventh thoracic vertebra.
Afferent fibers transmit sensory information from both the upper and lower surfaces of the diaphragm, as well as from the pericardium and mediastinal pleura and not from the liver capsule.
Phrenic Nerve
The phrenic nerves contain both efferent (motor) and afferent (sensory) fibers. (Option A ruled out) The efferent fibers provide the sole motor supply to the diaphragm muscle. (Option B ruled out)

The afferent fibers transmit sensory information to the central nervous system from the peritoneum covering the diaphragm's undersurface, the pleura on the diaphragm's upper surface, and the pericardium and mediastinal parietal pleura.
Paralysis of the phrenic nerve may result from pressure from malignant tumors in the mediastinum. (Option D ruled out)

Historically, surgical methods like crushing or sectioning the nerve in the neck were used to treat lung tuberculosis affecting the lower lobes, leading to diaphragm paralysis on that side. This causes the elevated, immobile dome of the diaphragm to provide rest to the affected lung.
The right phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5) has a more vertical and shorter course through the thorax compared to the left phrenic nerve.

Passes over left atrium and left ventricle

blocks.text: The endothoracic fascia is the layer encountered immediately before the parietal pleura during a pleural tap procedure. The endothoracic fascia lines the innermost intercostal muscle from inside and is fused with the parietal pleura, making it the last layer encountered before reaching the pleural space where fluid can be aspirated.
The order of structures punctured during a pleural tap, from superficial to deep:

items.text: Skin
Superficial fascia
Serratus anterior (1st muscle to get punctured)
External intercostal muscle
Internal intercostal muscle
Innermost intercostal muscle
Endothoracic fascia (Fused with parietal pleura)
Parietal pleura
Pleural fluid (to be aspirated)

blocks.text: The Chest X-ray shows a right sided pleural effusion for which the physician decides to perform thoracocentesis. The inferior border of the rib is the most important anatomical landmark to identify when performing a thoracentesis. This is because the intercostal neurovascular bundle (including the intercostal artery, vein, and nerve) runs along the inferior border of each rib.
By inserting the needle just above the superior border of the rib below the intended intercostal space, the risk of damaging these structures is minimized.
Pleural Tap
**Indications:** Used for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes in cases of pleural effusion. The fluid can be analyzed for various factors including culture, cytology, and biochemical analysis.
Empyema thoracis for diagnostic purpose
**Position:** The patient should be in a sitting position, leaning forward over a support.

**Site:** The procedure is performed at the 7th or 8th intercostal space, posteriorly, at the tip of the scapula. Needle insertion should target the upper edge/superior border of the rib in order to avoid injury to the neurovascular bundle which runs at the inferior margin of each rib.
**Needle:** A wide-bore needle (Abraham needle) is used under local anesthesia.
Complications

items.text: Infection
Dry tap or bloody tap
Sudden vagal shock
Pain and respiratory distress

blocks.text: The left atrium is obscured by the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk, and primarily forms part of the posterior surface, not the anterior surface.

**Anterior surface of heart (Sternocostal)** **Posterior View of Heart (Base)** The anterior surface consists mainly of the right atrium and right ventricle separated by the anterior atrioventricular groove (coronary sulcus). (Option B) The left auricle and left ventricle also contribute. (Option C & D) The right ventricle is separated from the left ventricle by the anterior interventricular groove.

The left atrium is obscured by the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk. The heart creates a cardiac notch on the mediastinal surface and anterior border of the left lung causing superficial cardiac dullness. The base of the heart is mainly formed by the left atrium (two-thirds) and right atrium (one-third). Major blood vessels like superior vena cava, ascending aorta, and pulmonary trunk attach to the base.

It is directed backwards and to the right, opposite the apex. The base lies opposite the apex and in front of thoracic vertebrae T5–T8 when lying down, descending to T6–T9 when standing. It is separated from the vertebral column by the oblique pericardial sinus, esophagus, and aorta.

The sternal angle (angle of Louis) is a palpable, transverse ridge on the sternum located approximately 5 cm below the suprasternal notch. It serves as a critical anatomical landmark for various significant structures and anatomical events.
These include:

items.text: The second costal cartilage articulates with the sternum at this level on both sides, making it a key reference point for counting ribs.
It corresponds to the level of the intervertebral disc between the T4 and T5 vertebrae.
A horizontal plane passing through this level divides the superior mediastinum from the inferior mediastinum.
The arch of the aorta both begins and ends at this level.
The trachea bifurcates into the right and left principal bronchus at this level.
The pulmonary trunk divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries here.
The upper border of the heart is located at this level.

blocks.text: The azygos vein arches over the root of the right lung and empties into the superior vena cava at this level. (Option B)

items.text: **Left atrium of the heart (Option A):** lies posteriorly and is located lower than the sternal angle, around the T6-T7 vertebral level.
**Origin of the thoracic duct (Option C):** is in the abdomen at the cisterna chyli, at the level of the L1-L2 vertebrae, far below the level of the sternal angle.
**Superior border of the aortic arch (Option D):** is located slightly above the level of the sternal angle, but its lower border (or the beginning and end of the arch) aligns with the T4-T5 level.

Mediastinum
The mediastinum is an anatomical region between the two lungs in the thoracic cavity.
**Boundaries:** Extends vertically from the thoracic inlet (superior thoracic aperture) to the diaphragm.

**Anterior** - Sternum **Posterior** - Thoracic vertebral column. The posterior boundary of the mediastinum is longer than the anterior because of the oblique alignment of the superior thoracic aperture and the posteroinferior curvature of the diaphragm. **Laterally** - mediastinal pleura, which are reflections of the parietal pleura.
It is divided into superior and inferior mediastinum by the sternal plane which passes horizontally from the manubriosternal joint to T4 to T5 vertebra.
Anatomical Divisions:
1. Superior Mediastinum
Located above the sternal angle (manubriosternal joint)
Contains critical structures such as:

items.text: Trachea and initial part of the bronchi

Thymus gland (or its remnants in adults)
Various nerves: vagus, phrenic, and cardiac nerves, left RLN
Lymph nodes
Thoracic duct

blocks.text: 2. Inferior Mediastinum
Located below the sternal angle and is further divided into anterior, middle, and posterior mediastinum.

blocks.text: The coronary arteries supply blood to specific regions of the heart. The right coronary artery (RCA) typically supplies the right atrium, right ventricle, part of the left ventricle, and the posterior one-third of the interventricular septum in individuals with right-dominant coronary circulation. The posterior descending artery (PDA) branches from the RCA in the right-dominant hearts and supplies the posterior part of the heart.

Coronary artery disease is a major cause of death worldwide. It is characterized by a reduced blood flow to the heart muscle (myocardium), depriving it of necessary oxygen. When a major coronary artery is suddenly blocked by an embolus (a plug or clot), the area of the heart muscle that relies on that artery for blood supply becomes ischemic. This lack of blood flow results in the death of the affected myocardial tissue due to necrosis.
The 3 most common sites of coronary artery occlusion are:

items.text: **1.** Anterior IV (LAD) branch of the LCA (40–50%).
**3.** Circumflex branch of the LCA (15–20%).

These regions would be affected by a blockage in the LAD, not the RCA.
The lateral wall of the left ventricle (Option B) is primarily supplied by the left circumflex (LCX) artery, a branch of the left coronary artery (LCA), and not RCA.
Cervical Pleura
Extends from the inner border of the 1st rib. Covers the apex of the lung. Passes downwards and medially to continue with the mediastinal pleura.
Pleural Cupola
Forms a cup-like dome over the apex of the lung. The summit of the dome reaches 2 to 3 cm higher than the medial third of the clavicle, at the level of the neck of the first rib.
Suprapleural Membrane (Sibson’s Fascia)

Covers the cervical pleura externally. A musculo-fascial expansion derived from the scalenus minimus muscle and endothoracic fascia. Extends from the tip of the transverse process of the 7th cervical vertebra to the inner border of the 1st rib. Medially continuous with the pretracheal fascia by the side of the trachea.
Relation to Structures
All structures related to the apex of the lung are superficial to the suprapleural membrane.

blocks.text: Arterial Supply of the Heart
The arterial supply to the heart is primarily provided by two main coronary arteries: the right coronary artery (RCA) and the left coronary artery (LCA).
These arteries originate from the aortic sinus.

items.text: **Right Conus Artery:** Supplies the pulmonary conus (infundibulum) and the upper right ventricle.
**Anterior Ventricular Branches:** 2 or 3 in number - supply the anterior surface of the right ventricle.
**Right Marginal Artery:** Largest of anterior ventricular branches - runs along the right margin of the heart towards the apex.

blocks.text: **Posterior Descending Artery (PDA) or the posterior interventricular artery:** Travels in the posterior interventricular groove, supplying the inferior wall of both ventricles and the posterior part of the interventricular septum. This artery often arises from the RCA but can also originate from the LCA in some individuals.
**Atrial Branches:** Supply the right atrium and contribute to the SA node in some individuals.

**Left Anterior Descending Artery (LAD):** Travels down the anterior interventricular groove to the heart’s apex. It supplies both ventricles and the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum.
**Left Circumflex Artery (LCX):** Circles around the left margin of the heart in the atrioventricular groove, giving off:

items.text: **Left Marginal Artery:** Supplies the left margin of the left ventricle.
**Anterior and Posterior Ventricular Branches:** Supply the left ventricle.
**Atrial Branches:** Supply the left atrium.

AVNRT is a common type of regular supraventricular tachycardia. It is characterized by a reentrant circuit involving fast and slow pathways, at the level of the AV node. Koch’s triangle is the anatomical region containing the AV node, which is critical in AVNRT.
**Pathways Involved:**

items.text: **Slow pathway:** posterior to the AV node.
**Fast pathway:** anterior nodal extension.

blocks.text: **Anatomical Landmark: Triangle of Koch:** Used for catheter ablation (CA), bordered by:

items.text: **Coronary sinus ostium** (inferiorly).
**Septal leaflet of tricuspid valve** (anteriorly).
**Tendon of Todaro** (posterosuperiorly).

blocks.text: **Circuit Involvement:** Limited to the AV node and surrounding myocardium. May extend beyond the AV node, including parts of the tricuspid and mitral vestibules.

**Treatment:** Catheter ablation targets the slow (Koch’s Triangle) and fast pathways to interrupt the reentrant circuit. Crista terminalis, His bundle, and Right atrial appendage are not involved in AVNRT. (Options A, B, and D).
The Triangle of Koch is situated on the right atrial aspect of the interatrial septum.
**Boundaries:**

items.text: Opening of the coronary sinus
The Tendon of Todaro - a collagenous subendocardial band - runs from the central fibrous body to the Eustachian ridge - a part of the fibrous skeleton of the heart.
Septal tricuspid leaflet

blocks.text: **Importance:** It helps to localize the AV node - present at the apex of Koch’s triangle.
Localising the AV node is important to safely perform radiofrequency catheter ablation within the right atrium in cases of AVNRT.
**Sinoatrial node (Option A):** is located in the upper part of the right atrium, near the opening of the superior vena cava, not in Koch's triangle.

**While the bundle of His (Option C):** is anatomically close to the AV node, it is not typically found at the apex of Koch's triangle. It emerges from the AV node and penetrates the cardiac skeleton.
**Right bundle branch (Option D):** is a continuation of the bundle of His and is found in the interventricular septum, not in Koch's triangle.

items.text: **Right Border:** Formed by the right atrium. Extends from the opening of the superior vena cava (SVC) to the inferior vena cava (IVC).

**Upper Border:** Formed mainly by the left atrium. Partly by the right atrium. Also by the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.

blocks.text: Pleura Structure and Function
Visceral Pleura
Surrounds lung tissue. Composed of a single mesothelial cell layer. Blood supply from bronchial arteries.
Parietal Pleura
Lines the inner chest wall. Contains stomata that drain pleural fluid into lymphatic capillaries. Connective tissue present; innervated by sensory nerve fibers.
Pleural Fluid

items.text: **Normal Volume:** 0.1 to 0.2 mL/kg.
**Inflow Rate:** 0.5 mL/hr in adults.
**Maximal Removal Rate:** 0.28 mL/kg/hr.

blocks.text: Accumulates when inflow exceeds removal (due to increased plasma filtration or impaired lymphatic drainage).
Lymphatic Drainage

Lymph drains into regional lymph nodes along the sternum or vertebra, then into the thoracic and right lymphatic ducts. Lymphatic vessels are 10-12 µm in diameter, large enough for intact erythrocytes.
Innervation
Visceral Pleura
No connective tissue; innervated by the vagus nerve, insensitive to pain.
Parietal Pleura
Connective tissue; innervated by intercostal nerves and phrenic nerve.
**Phrenic Nerve:** Predominantly innervates the central diaphragmatic region, referred pain to the ipsilateral shoulder.
Pleural Membrane Function
Allows frictionless movement of the lungs relative to the chest wall during respiration.
**Inspiration:** Negative pressure in the pleural space leads to lung expansion, allowing air to enter the lungs
Atrioventricular (Coronary) Sulcus separates the atria from the ventricles and contains the major coronary arteries.
Grooves of the Heart
**Interatrial Sulcus (of Waterston):** Separates the two atria. (Option A)

**Atrioventricular (Coronary) Sulcus:** Separates the atria from the ventricles. Contains major coronary arteries. Descends obliquely on the anterior surface, separating the right atrium and its auricle from the right ventricle. Curves around the left border and connects with the inferior part. The left anterior part of the AV groove between the left auricle and left ventricle, houses the circumflex branch of the left coronary artery. The posterior part of the AV groove lies between the base and the diaphragmatic surface of the heart, containing the coronary sinus.

**Anterior Interventricular Sulcus: (Option C)** Located near the left border of the heart on the sternocostal surface. Extends from the atrioventricular sulcus to the notch at the cardiac apex. Contains the anterior interventricular artery and the great cardiac vein.

**Inferior Interventricular Sulcus: (Option D)** Closer to the midpoint of the ventricular mass on the diaphragmatic surface. Extends from the atrioventricular sulcus to the notch at the cardiac apex. Contains the posterior interventricular artery and the middle cardiac vein.

blocks.text: The presence of distended chest wall veins (collaterals) is highly indicative of increased venous pressure, commonly associated with superior vena cava (SVC) obstruction. In this case, the history of a mediastinal mass and metastasis suggests that the mass is compressing the SVC, leading to venous obstruction.
This obstruction can cause the characteristic collateral circulation (distended chest wall veins) to develop, as the body attempts to reroute blood flow to bypass the obstruction.
The illustration below shows signs of SVC obstruction

**Right heart failure (Option A):** While this can cause jugular distension, it typically does not lead to the development of prominent chest wall collaterals without other signs of systemic congestion.
**Pulmonary embolism (Option C):** This may cause acute respiratory distress but does not typically lead to distended chest wall veins or collaterals.

**Thoracic aortic aneurysm (Option D):** This may cause symptoms related to compression of surrounding structures but does not specifically account for the venous distension seen with SVC obstruction.

If the pleural effusion fluid is chylous (chyle), it indicates leakage of lymphatic fluid, often due to disruption or injury to the thoracic duct. Chylothorax is a condition where chyle accumulates in the pleural space, leading to pleural effusion. The thoracic duct drains lymph into the junction of the left subclavian vein and left internal jugular vein.
Thoracic duct

The thoracic duct starts as the cisterna chyli in the abdomen at the lower border of the T12 vertebra. It ascends through the aortic opening of the diaphragm. It initially runs on the right side of the descending aorta in the posterior mediastinum. At the T4 vertebra, it crosses from the right to the left side behind the esophagus. It continues upward along the left border of the esophagus to the root of the neck.

At the root of the neck, it arches laterally at the C7 vertebra, in front of the vertebral arteries and behind the carotid system. The duct collects lymph from the left jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal trunks. It descends in front of the first part of the left subclavian artery.
It ends by draining into the junction of the left subclavian vein and the left internal jugular vein. (Option A, C, & D ruled out)
The thoracic duct carries lymph from the lower limbs, pelvic cavity, abdominal cavity, and the left side of the thorax, head, neck, and arm.
The right lymphatic duct does not drain the right abdomen; this region is typically drained by the thoracic duct, which handles lymph from the lower half of the body, including the abdomen.
Right Lymphatic Duct

The right lymphatic duct may form from the convergence of the right jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal trunks. These trunks drain lymph from the right side of the head and neck, the right upper limb, and the right side of the thorax. When present, the right lymphatic duct is approximately 0.5 inches (1.3 cm) long. It opens into the beginning of the right brachiocephalic vein.
Alternatively, the lymphatic trunks may drain directly into the major veins at the root of the neck.

Subcostal neuralgia is caused by irritation or compression of the T12 (subcostal) nerve, which provides sensory innervation to the skin of the upper abdomen below the ribcage. It typically presents with sharp, localized pain along the costal margin, especially aggravated by deep breathing or movement (such as twisting or bending). The pain can be unilateral, as seen in this patient.

The absence of gastrointestinal symptoms (like nausea, vomiting, or changes in bowel habits), along with localized tenderness over the right costal margin, supports the diagnosis of subcostal neuralgia. Subcostal neuralgia can be caused by various factors, including nerve compression, inflammation, or irritation of the intercostal nerves. It may also follow trauma, surgical procedures (especially abdominal surgeries), or infections.

The condition can sometimes occur without any obvious underlying cause. It is typically managed with pain relief, such as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and physical therapy to help relieve nerve compression. The intercostal nerves are part of the somatic nervous system and arise from the ventral rami of the T1-T11 spinal nerves.
The 12th spinal nerve does not contribute to the intercostal nerves, but rather forms the subcostal nerve.

items.text: **Origin:** The intercostal nerves are derived from the ventral rami of the thoracic spinal nerves (T1-T11).

**Course:** These nerves travel along the intercostal spaces between the ribs, passing laterally and then anteriorly toward the sternum. They travel in the costal groove on the inferior aspect of each rib, along with the intercostal artery and vein. The nerves are positioned in the neurovascular bundle along the inferior border of each rib, with the vein superior, the artery in the middle, and the nerve inferior.
**Branches:** Each intercostal nerve gives off several branches:
**Lateral cutaneous branch:** Provides sensory innervation to the skin of the lateral chest and upper abdomen.
**Anterior cutaneous branch:** Supplies the skin over the anterior chest wall.
**Muscular branches:** Innervate the intercostal muscles, transversus thoracis, and sometimes the serratus anterior muscle.
**Rami communicantes:** Connect the intercostal nerve to the sympathetic trunk.

**Function:** Motor: To the intercostal muscles (which aid in respiration). Sensory: To the skin of the chest, abdomen, and parts of the back. Sympathetic: To the sweat glands and blood vessels in the region.
**T12 (Subcostal Nerve):** The T12 nerve (subcostal nerve) runs below the 12th rib and supplies the muscles of the anterior abdominal wall and skin just below the costal margin.

blocks.text: **Acute cholecystitis (Option A):** typically presents with right upper quadrant pain that is often associated with nausea, vomiting, and fever. **Appendicitis (Option C):** typically starts with periumbilical pain that eventually migrates to the right lower quadrant. It is also accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and fever, which this patient does not have. The pain in appendicitis is generally deep and constant, not related to movement.

**Peptic ulcer disease (Option D):** may present with epigastric pain and is often aggravated by food or empty stomach. However, the pain tends to be dull and burning, rather than sharp and localized along the rib margin. The absence of nausea, vomiting, and changes in appetite makes this diagnosis less likely.

The subclavian vein is a key vessel in the venous system that drains blood from the upper limb, the neck, and part of the chest. It is located in the thoracic region and plays a crucial role in returning deoxygenated blood to the heart.
1. Location and Course:

The subclavian vein is positioned deep to the clavicle (collarbone) and lies within the thoracic inlet, a narrow space between the neck and the chest. It runs laterally and horizontally beneath the clavicle, crossing the first rib and passing anterior to the anterior scalene muscle. It continues to run towards the right or left sternoclavicular joint, where it drains into the brachiocephalic vein on both sides (right and left).
2. Relations:

items.text: **Posterior Relations:** The subclavian vein is located anterior to the subclavian artery. The clavicle (collarbone) lies above the vein, and it is closely associated with the sternoclavicular joint and muscles like the pectoralis minor.

**Anterior Relations:** The subclavian vein runs posterior to the anterior scalene muscle, which separates it from the subclavian artery. The vein is also related to the first rib, which lies beneath it.
**Medial Relations:** On the medial side, it is adjacent to the brachiocephalic vein.

**Lateral Relations:** The vein continues laterally and joins the internal jugular vein to form the brachiocephalic vein. The thoracic duct (on the left side) drains into the subclavian vein near the junction of the internal jugular vein. The subclavian vein is larger and more anterior and superficial than the subclavian artery.

blocks.text: 3. Anatomy:

items.text: **Right subclavian vein:** It drains into the right brachiocephalic vein.
**Left subclavian vein:** It drains into the left brachiocephalic vein.
**Thoracic duct:** The thoracic duct drains lymph from the left side of the body into the left subclavian vein near its junction with the internal jugular vein.

blocks.text: 4. Clinical Relevance:

The subclavian vein is often used for central venous catheter insertion, central venous pressure monitoring. Subclavian vein thrombosis (also known as Paget-Schroetter syndrome) can occur due to repetitive trauma, leading to clots, especially in athletes or individuals with certain anatomical predispositions.

items.text: **A. Superior vena cava:** The superior vena cava is a large vein that carries deoxygenated blood from the upper half of the body to the right atrium of the heart. It is located anterior and slightly to the right of the ascending aorta.
**B. Ascending aorta:** The ascending aorta arises from the left ventricle of the heart and is the initial portion of the aorta that moves upward before arching.

**C. Pulmonary Trunk:** The pulmonary trunk is the vessel that arises from the right ventricle and bifurcates into the left and right pulmonary arteries, which carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs. It is positioned anterior to the ascending aorta and the superior vena cava.

**D. Descending Aorta:** The descending aorta continues from the aortic arch and runs downwards behind the heart, supplying blood to the lower parts of the body. It is located posterior to the heart and more to the left in the thoracic cavity.

Foramen ovale does not anatomically close within 3 to 5 days. Functional closure occurs soon after birth due to increased left atrial pressure, but anatomical closure (fusion of the septum primum and septum secundum) takes months to years. In some individuals, it may persist as a patent foramen ovale (PFO).

Anatomical closure of ductus venosus is by 2 to 3 weeks (option B): The ductus venosus shunts oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava in fetal circulation. After birth, it functionally closes within hours and anatomically closes in 2 to 3 weeks, forming the ligamentum venosum.
Formation of the Interatrial Septum:

Septum Primum Formed as a sickle-shaped fold from the roof and dorsal wall of the primitive atrium due to pressure from the bulbus cordis. Grows downward toward the atrioventricular (AV) canal and septum intermedium, fusing with the latter.
Ostium Primum Before the septum primum reaches and fuses with the septum intermedium, a gap (foramen primum) allows blood flow between the right and left atria.
Ostium Secundum Upper part of the septum primum breaks down, creating a new gap (foramen secundum) before the foramen primum closes. The septum primum now has a free upper edge.
Septum Secundum Grows down from the roof of the atrial chamber, to the right of the septum primum, overlapping the free upper edge of the septum primum as it grows.
Foramen Ovale Formation Overlapping septa create the foramen ovale, allowing blood to flow from right to left atrium during fetal life, preventing left-to-right flow. Patent throughout fetal life.

Obliteration of Foramen Ovale Post-birth, the left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs, increasing pressure in this chamber greater than the right atrium, causing fusion of the septum primum and septum secundum, closing the foramen ovale.

Annulus ovalis (adults) corresponds to the lower free edge of the septum secundum, while the fossa ovalis represents the septum primum. Right umbilical vein is absent after birth (option C): The right umbilical vein degenerates during fetal life, leaving only the left umbilical vein to carry blood from the placenta. After birth, the left umbilical vein also closes, forming the ligamentum teres (round ligament of the liver).

Anatomical closure of ductus arteriosus is by 2 to 3 weeks (option D): The ductus arteriosus functionally closes within 24 to 48 hours due to oxygenation and prostaglandin metabolism. Anatomical closure occurs by 2 to 3 weeks, forming the ligamentum arteriosum.

The round structure just in front of the vertebral column is descending aorta, slightly towards the left. The descending aorta is located posterior to the diaphragm, in the midline of the body. It is a continuation of the thoracic aorta and descends along the vertebral column in the posterior mediastinum before entering the abdominal cavity. In the abdominal cavity, it descends along the posterior wall, slightly to the left of the midline, and gives off branches to the abdominal organs.
Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Option B -** Superior vena cava: The superior vena cava, found in the superior mediastinum, enters the right atrium of the heart. It is not visible in abdominal cavity cross-sections.

**Option C -** Inferior vena cava: The inferior vena cava enters the right atrium from the posterior mediastinum, traveling along the back of the abdominal wall to the right of the midline, collecting blood from the lower body and abdominal organs.

**Option D -** Ascending aorta: The ascending aorta begins at the left ventricle, ascends to the superior mediastinum, and branches into the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, and left subclavian artery.

blocks.text: It gives rise to the circumflex coronary branch. This statement is false. The right coronary artery does not typically give rise to the circumflex coronary branch. The circumflex branch is a branch of the left coronary artery. It wraps around the left side of the heart and supplies blood to the left atrium and portions of the left ventricle.
Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Option A -** Its diameter is less than the left coronary artery. This statement is generally true. Left coronary artery (LCA) typically has a slightly larger diameter than the the right coronary artery (RCA)

**Option B -** It arises from the anterior aortic sinus. This statement is true. The right coronary artery originates from the right aortic sinus, which is one of the three aortic sinuses located at the base of the aorta.
**Option D -** Right conal artery is its first branch. This statement is true. The right conal artery is indeed the first branch of the right coronary artery.

blocks.text: The thoracolumbar fascia (TLF) is composed of three layers (anterior, middle, and posterior) in the lumbar region, not four. It provides attachment for various muscles and encloses the intrinsic back muscles.

The joint between the attachment of the 8th and 9th rib to the 7th rib is classified as a synovial joint. Synovial joints are characterized by the presence of a joint cavity filled with synovial fluid, which allows for smooth movement between the articulating surfaces.
Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Option A -** Fibrocartilaginous joint: Fibrocartilaginous joints, like intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis, provide stability with limited movement due to fibrocartilage between bones.
**Option B -** Symphyseal joint: Symphyseal joints, featuring hyaline and fibrocartilage, allow limited movement and are seen in the pubic symphysis and intervertebral discs.

**Option D -** Fibrous joint: Fibrous joints, like skull sutures, typically allow minimal movement due to fibrous connective tissue. However, the joint between the 8th and 9th rib attachment to the 7th rib permits movement and isn't solely fibrous.
